Figure 12 displays a functional diagram for COSMOS' OTB.

caption_chunks.context: In order to expose and check the SRAM, the experiment needs to power the SRAM and read and write to the SRAM. These functions are specific enough so that subsystems can be designed but broad enough that the design is not dictated by the functional decomposition.

caption_chunks.context: As the need for a simple build template for CubeSats was identified at USNA, the Parkinson Sat 1U (PSAT1U) system, named for the inventor of the Global Positioning System (GPS) was developed. Its purpose is to serve as a modular architecture with easily accessible parts that enables a complete satellite bus development in three weeks. This allows students to focus on designing and implementing their preferred on-board payload and mission systems without spending undue time carrying out trade studies on well understood subsystems and components. caption_chunks.context: EOL. The initial I&T phase concerns the integration and testing operations conducted prior to launch, while the LEOP encompasses the launch, the release into the target orbit, the deployment, the detumbling, and the commissioning phases. The Operational Phase is comprised of two distinct sub-phases. During the first sub-phase, environmental data is collected and a database on Earth mapping is created for the purpose of implementing navigation by landmark. In the subsequent sub-phase, while the collection of environmental parameters for Earth Observation (EO) purposes is continued, the deep space technologies are tested. Finally, the EOL phase involves de-orbiting, passivation and re-entry. The figure 4.15 shows a visual representation of ConOps.

caption_chunks.context: A Real-Time Operating System provides the deterministic behaviour that a critical system requires to meet hard deadlines. The design philosophy behind the UWE-5 embedded software strives to achieve welldefined layers that perform functionalities and/or services to the other layers. The mission code layer is separated from the RTOS layer using an Operating System Abstraction Layer (OSAL), which is composed of the well-known POSIX threading APIs (pthreads) [13]. A special layer, called the KronOS Task-Manager, extends the FreeRTOS scheduler with functionality for dynamic resource allocation, load balancing, and fault management. elements.name: MO-1: Measure the flux of secondary neutrons and gamma rays produced by cosmic ray interactions in Low Earth Orbit as a function of time, geomagnetic latitude, and altitude (location based data).
MO-2: Measure secondary neutron and gamma ray flux variations before, during, and after solar energetic particle (SEP) events (event based data).

MSC-1: The mission shall collect neutron fluxes over one of Earth’s poles (latitudes >66°N or <−66°S), subdivided into three latitude bands: 66°–74°, 74°–82°, and 82°–90°. The accumulated neutron count within each band must have a maximum relative uncertainty of 10% (TBC).

FSC-1: The mission shall collect at least two sets of 10,000 accumulated neutron counts in each of the following regions: the North Pole, the South Pole (Latitudes >66°N and <−66°S), and the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), with each set separated by at least 3-6 months to enable temporal analysis of the neutron environment in low Earth orbit.

ESC-1: The mission shall collect at least 10,000 accumulated neutron counts in each of the following regions: the North Pole, the South Pole, and the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), at two different altitudes separated by at least 50 km (at least 60,000 counts total). The two altitude-based data sets for each region shall be collected within 40 days of each other.

MSC-2: Collect neutron and gamma ray flux before, during, and after a single solar energetic particle (SEP) event. For the SEP event of interest, the 'before' and 'after' data must be collected within 40 days of the event, and no other SEP event should occur between the 'before' and 'after' data periods.

FSC-2: Collect neutron and gamma ray flux before, during, and after at least two distinct solar energetic particle (SEP) events during the mission. For each SEP event of interest, the 'before' and 'after' data must be collected within 40 days of the event, and no other SEP event should occur between the 'before' and 'after' data periods.

other_visible_labels: The Neutron-2 mission aims to study neutron and gamma-ray fluxes as a function of time, geomagnetic position (lat, lon, alt), and solar activity to gain insights into cosmic ray interactions, solar particle events, and space weather in LEO to make space exploration safer for all.

caption_chunks.caption: Figure 2.5. SysML diagram categories supporting MBSE (No Magic, 2022).
caption_chunks.context: SysML supports diverse viewpoints through nine diagram types grouped into four primary categories: structure, behavior, requirements, and parametrics. Figure 2.5 shows the hierarchical classification of these diagram types, each supporting different aspects of the system specification and lifecycle alignment (No Magic, 2022). For example, Block Definition Diagrams (BDDs) and Internal Block Diagrams (IBDs) are used to describe static structure and internal interactions. Techniques such as the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Quality Function Deployment (QFD), Binary Search Tree (BST), and MoSCoW provide structured methods for comparing needs based on utility, feasibility, or complexity (Millet, 2005). caption_chunks.caption: Figure 2. SysML model creation methodology.
caption_chunks.context: To create a model from an existing DSM representation, the first step was to make the DSM symmetric by assuming any interaction to be bidirectional, a simplifying assumption given that it is not clear if a directional flow would reduce the interaction complexity. The parts were then divided into subsystems and an IBD was created for each subsystem depicting the interactions between the different parts of the subsystem. The interactions between parts of different subsystems were depicted as interactions between the subsystem themselves. This methodology renders the external interaction of the subsystems $ \gamma_{i m} $ equal to zero. An illustration of the process can be seen in Figure 2.

caption_chunks.caption: Figure 4.15: Interaction between CSM, STK and Excel for scenario 2
caption_chunks.context: In this scenario, a CubeSat namely "ADSLSat" is created using classical coordinates. By utilizing the AdvCAT object of STK, potential close proximity and encounters between "ADSLSat" and other two-line element (TLE) sets have been calculated. The scenario resides under Behavior->System Behavior Simulation package in the CubeSat-SSA system model and can be run through an executable SysML state machine diagram. System context for this scenario is "Close Approach". The scenario automatically produces two reports namely "Close Approach By Min Range" and "Encounter Warnings". The reports are also saved in separate Excel files which can be reincorporated into the model through excel sync capability of cameo simulation toolkit. Figure 4.15 shows the interaction between CSM, STK and Excel for Scenario 2.

caption_chunks.caption: Figure 4.19: Scenario 3 run through SysML Activity Diagram
caption_chunks.context: As the output value of the MATALB function i.e. relevance percentage used as input to the CubeSat-SSA System Model owned value property relevance_percentage, Operational Requirements-03 can be checked for verification. This is because OpReq03 has a satisfy relationship with the "relevance_percantage". When the "relevance_percantage" value property automatically populated, it checks whether it satisfies the requirement specified value or not. If it satisfy the linked requirement, it shows green color in the variable section of CST. If it does not satisfy the requirement, it shows red color (Figure 4.21) and a message (Figure 4.20) in the CST's console panel.

caption_chunks.context: The Power subsystem calculates and stores the time history of the battery depth of discharge. The subsystem uses the power usage history and the size of the batteries to determine the time history of the battery depth of discharge and stores the result as state variables.

caption_chunks.context: In the original 480 second simulation, the satellite did not perform a data downlink maneuver due to inadequate simulation time. At this point, HSF finds the conditions favorable to schedule a communication downlink task. Five successive downlink tasks are performed until the SSDR has downlinked all data. At this point, no additional data is stored.

caption_chunks.caption: Figure 1. Satlet concept development
caption_chunks.context: The overall concept for the methodology is shown in Figure 1. Preliminary scoping and requirements analysis are used to define a manageable exploration problem. The objective for the exploration is the expected value of producing a particular architecture, based on the revenue of successfully completing a mission minus the cost of the aggregate system. This will be more thoroughly discussed in Sections A-C. The tradespace for the problem is captured using the SysML modeling language (described in Section D). Finally, the automated trade space exploration (described in Section E) takes the objective function, mission requirements, and scoped trade space as inputs and then generates and evaluates a large number of potential cellularized architectures.

caption_chunks.context: The architecture described in this work features a classic, initial value approach to state variable propagation, whereby the differential equations describing time-evolution of the state variables are integrated using numerical methods over a finite time interval. This process continues for the duration of the simulation, building a state variable matrix that describes the system over the period of interest. Illustration of a generic state variable analysis, in block diagram form, is shown in figure 1, from which the architecture in this work is built.

caption_chunks.caption: Fig. 2: SysML diagram of top-level architecture showing a selection of internal properties
caption_chunks.context: The dynamic behaviour of a satellite in LEO is typically non-linear over a number of length-scales. For example, environmental perturbations contribute to secular variation in the orbital dynamics over periods of days and months, motion of the satellite about the earth occurs over minutes and data collection and transmission can take place over a period of seconds. Within this work the long-term dynamics are captured in a Lifetime model, which conducts analysis over the complete mission, whilst dynamics related to the other two scales are analysed over a number of orbits within an Operations model, consisting of higher detail and fidelity. caption_chunks.caption: Figure 5. Space Environment Framework
caption_chunks.context: The SysML Internal Block Diagram, in Figure 5, provides the basis for modeling both the propagation of radio waves and also the trapping of ionospheric particles. Each aspect of the Earth's atmosphere has different effects on the propagation of radio waves. Water vapor is primarily concentrated in the troposphere and absorbs radio waves at various frequencies. The ionosphere contains charged elements that interact with radio waves. Both these factors influence the transmission of communication signals between the satellite and ground station. It also contains the primary science target of the mission: a series of trapped plasma formations.

caption_chunks.context: A SysML model interfaced with STK, enables satellite designers to consider how design parameters, such as satellite battery, radio, and ground station networks influence the potential to achieve the Mission Objectives. Furthermore, spacecraft operational planning can be simulated and optimized more accurately with SysML interfaced with STK. This modeling capability can also enable satellite operators to schedule satellite operations considering position, attitude, on-board energy, data, and thermal states.

caption_chunks.context: Fig. 1: Inter-dependencies between Architectural model and Operational model. and space mission design. This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the proposed operational scenario modeling coupled with architectural definition; while Section 3 compares the two case studies as an end-to-end validation of the proposed methodology. Section 4 discusses the main outcomes of this work and lessons learned. Finally, Section 5 summarizes the proposed work and provides directions for future work. 2 Proposed Operations modeling This section presents a modeling approach for ConOps and OMs as integral part of the system architecture modeling within the newly developed Modeling & Simulation Architecture for integrated Complex systems (MOSAiC) MBSE framework [11, 19]. The methodology builds upon the ARCADIA method and uses the Capella toolset, while proposing the co-development of system behavior and architecture through formal abstractions and state-based modeling. Unlike conventional practices where to the authors' best knowledge mostly only architectural models are developed, the proposed approach establishes a continuous and traceable linkage between system structure and mission execution logic, ensuring consistency throughout the lifecycle. 2.1 Methodological Foundations The modeling process follows ARCADIA's layered abstraction, beginning with Operational Analysis (OA), which defines mission goals and stakeholder interactions, and advancing through System Analysis (SA), Logical Architecture (LA), and Physical Architecture (PA) [4]. At each stage, the architecture is incrementally refined - from functional groupings to subsystem allocations and finally to component - level instantiations. ConOps elements are modeled concurrently with this structural development. Mission phases - such as launch, commissioning, or nominal operations - define the operational timeline. Within each phase, the system may adopt different internal configurations or behaviors - captured as Operating Modes. These OMs, defined through Capella's state machine diagrams, represent both the system's status (e.g., Safe Mode, Science Mode) and the conditions under which transitions occur (e.g., power thresholds, visibility events, fault recovery). At the subsystem level, Modes represent variations in functional behavior (e.g., Payload Active, TTC Idle) based on the current mission phase and system objectives. Using add-ons like the Property Values Management Tool (PVMT) [20] within Capella, quantitative data such as power consumption and relative margins are assigned to components and subsystems based on their active mode. These parameters are crucial for performance simulations and for assessing the validity of operational scenarios within design constraints. The tight coupling between state-based logic and physical properties allows designers to directly simulate mission execution and verify design compliance at early stages $ ^{1} $ $ ^{1} $All data and models are available in a public repository under GPLv3 license at [19].

caption_chunks.context: 2.2 Interconnection Between Architectural and Operational Models The core of the proposed methodology is its emphasis on the interconnection between the architectural and operational models. This relationship is captured in a layered model framework (see Fig. 1), which illustrates how operational definitions and architectural abstractions evolve in parallel, influencing and constraining one another across the system lifecycle. On the architectural side, the model progresses from OA through SA, LA, and PA. Each level introduces greater design specificity - from abstract functions to logical subsystems to physical components. In parallel, the operational model introduces corresponding layers of behavioral detail: from broad ConOps phases to detailed system modes and subsystem-level variations. This bidirectional structure supports both design derivation and behavioral execution. The required operations "drive the design of" the architecture by defining available capabilities and constraints; conversely, the architectural elements "execute" the operations, activating specific functions and behaviors in time. For instance, an OM such as "Science Acquisition" will dictate the active configuration of subsystems, turning on payload components, activating data storage, and powering down nonessential services. These behavioral requirements must be anticipated and satisfied by the architectural layout defined at the LA and PA levels. Capella enables this integration through explicit cross-model references. OMs are not modeled in isolation; rather, they are embedded in the same environment as architectural elements, allowing mode-specific behavior to be tied directly to component definitions and mission scenarios. Transitions between modes (and thus different behaviors that a component might have) are governed by environmental or system triggers - visibility conditions, battery levels, or ground station access and reflect the actual execution environment of the spacecraft. Because these transitions are stored alongside component-level data and system structure, simulations can leverage the complete model for performance assessment. 3 Case studies comparison 3.1 Satellite Case Study To validate this integrated modeling methodology, it was firstly applied to the FIRE-EYE mission - a multisatellite CubeSat constellation designed for near-realtime wildfire monitoring in the Mediterranean region, already presented in a preparatory work [11]. The mission was selected as a representative case due to its operational complexity, resource constraints, and need for mode-driven autonomy across multiple mission phases. The system consists of 48 16U CubeSats equipped with multi-spectral imaging payloads. Each satellite operates autonomously and undergoes a structured lifecycle composed of launch, commissioning, nominal operation, science acquisition, and data transmission phases. These phases were modeled as discrete ConOps stages, each linked to specific OMs that reflected the system's intended behavior. In the OA phase, the primary stakeholders - including civil protection agencies, regional authorities, and the mission operators - were modeled with their associated operational capabilities, as shown in Fig. 2. Fig. 2: Main project capabilities and Stakeholders identification A primary operational capability was identified to represent the mission goal: [SCI-OBJ] To near-realtime monitor wildfire in the Mediterranean area. This capability encompasses the system's core function of detecting, mapping, and alerting wildfire events with minimal latency. In parallel, a second capability was defined: [STANDARD] Mission Lifecycle, which represents the set of standardized processes and lifecycle phases required to design, develop, launch, operate, and dispose of the space segment. This capability supports alignment with established space mission development practices (e.g., ECSS standards) and enables long-term roadmapping. Subsequently, stakeholder activities and interactions were modeled to clarify user needs and objectives, as shown in Fig. 3. The Capella OA enables the creation of a domain model - abstracted from the future system to focus on the stakeholders' real-world needs, independently of any technical implementation [21]. Fig. 3: FireEYE Operational Architecture. These activities, such as "to detect wildfires" or "to provide alerts and situational awareness", were used to drive the system analysis and function breakdown.

Another key result is the generalization of Operating Modes (OMs) for CubeSats by identifying common attributes and transition criteria among different Low Earth Orbit (LEO) CubeSat Concepts of Operations (ConOps's). This allows mission scenarios to be defined by modifying OM attributes, regardless of the data format. Additionally, a specialized parser created for model files allows for automatic updates to the model itself, such as after simulation or parameter optimization phases. A proof of concept is demonstrated using the SysML model of the "The White Compass (TWC)" theoretical mission, integrated with the Nanostar Software Suite (NSS) [12, 13] analysis tools through a dedicated parser, successfully producing power and data budgets $ ^{1} $ . 3 Systems and Unified Modelling Languages The Unified Modelling Language (UML) [14], developed in the late 1980s and early 1990s, quickly became a leading modeling language, primarily used for software development [15]. In the early 2000s, the Systems Modelling Language (SysML) [16] was introduced by the Object Management Group (OMG), International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE), and other collaborators as a specialized extension of UML tailored for Systems Engineering applications, particularly for modeling complex physical systems. A comprehensive discussion of SE methodologies with SysML can be found in Weilkiens [15]. Key concepts from UML and SysML that are critical to understanding this work are outlined below. 3.1 UML Classes A core element of object-oriented modeling, classes define both the structure and behavior of objects that share similar characteristics. Classes are characterized by their attributes (structure) and operations (behavior) and are represented through class diagrams. These diagrams can depict software components or real-world objects, at varying levels of abstraction [15]. Fig. 2: Example of a UML class and object, illustrating inherited attributes and operations. Attributes Attributes specify the properties that define a model, which classes inherit. These properties include visibility, name, type, and multiplicity (the number of instances associated with each class) [15]. Associations Associations describe relationships between two classes. Types of associations include aggregation (which represents a whole-part hierarchy) and composition (a whole-part hierarchy where parts cannot exist independently of the whole) [15]. Generalizations Generalizations create hierarchies between a general superclass and a more specific subclass [15]. The subclass represents a more specialized form of the superclass (e.g., cat, dog, and horse are subclasses of the animal superclass) .

In the early 2000s, the Systems Modelling Language (SysML) [16] was introduced by the Object Management Group (OMG), International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE), and other collaborators as a specialized extension of UML tailored for Systems Engineering applications, particularly for modeling complex physical systems. A comprehensive discussion of SE methodologies with SysML can be found in Weilkiens [15]. Key concepts from UML and SysML that are critical to understanding this work are outlined below. 3.1 UML Classes A core element of object-oriented modeling, classes define both the structure and behavior of objects that share similar characteristics. Classes are characterized by their attributes (structure) and operations (behavior) and are represented through class diagrams. These diagrams can depict software components or real-world objects, at varying levels of abstraction [15]. Fig. 2: Example of a UML class and object, illustrating inherited attributes and operations. Attributes Attributes specify the properties that define a model, which classes inherit. These properties include visibility, name, type, and multiplicity (the number of instances associated with each class) [15]. Associations Associations describe relationships between two classes. Types of associations include aggregation (which represents a whole-part hierarchy) and composition (a whole-part hierarchy where parts cannot exist independently of the whole) [15]. Generalizations Generalizations create hierarchies between a general superclass and a more specific subclass [15]. The subclass represents a more specialized form of the superclass (e.g., cat, dog, and horse are subclasses of the animal superclass) .

The keyword > is used to indicate the base element that is being extended [15]. (a) (b) Fig. 4: Examples of UML stereotypes. (a) Example of stereotype definition. (b) Example of stereotype application. 3.2 SysML Blocks and Block Definition Diagrams In SysML, UML classes are referred to as blocks, and UML class diagrams are represented as Block Definition Diagrams (BDDs). SysML expands the scope of UML classes, enabling the modeling of system structures across multiple domains beyond software [15]. Value Types, Units, and Dimensions A value type is a specialized form of UML data type that includes both a unit and a dimension. Units describe the physical measurement units, while dimensions specify the quantities associated with those units [15]. Requirements and Requirement Diagrams SysML introduces the concept of requirements, which define the conditions that a system must satisfy. These are illustrated in requirement diagrams [15]. 4 Stereotypes application Several studies (e.g., Bajaj et al. [17] and Spangelo et al. [18]) have introduced tools that attempt to address some of the integration challenges between SysML models and domain-specific simulation tools. Specifically, they enable SysML models to interface with specialized simulation environments, thereby streamlining the design and analysis process. Such works, while providing useful information about the use of SysML as an interface between external databases and external simulation tools, require the use of proprietary tools. Two main requirements have been imposed for the formalization presented in [9]: the exclusive use of open-source tools, following the principle of Open Science, and the use of a single model, inclusive of all mission parameters to facilitate the PD phase of a CubeSat without the need to refer to an external database. In the meantime, the demand for an open-source CubeSat design resulted in several initiatives, e.g.: the Libre Space Foundation [19]: University of Patras Satellite (UPSat) [20]; LibreCube [21]; Satellite Networked Open Ground Stations (SatNOGS) [22]; ArduSat [23]; Open Source CubeSat Workshop [24]; Nanostar Software Suite (NSS) [12, 13]. To the best of the authors' knowledge, however, no open-source framework existed that fully addressed all the challenges and requirements outlined in this research. The question to be answered by the proposed formalization was then whether it was possible to use MBSE as a frontend for the entire design cycle of a CubeSat, with the exclusive use of open-source tools. With this in mind, SysML has been chosen as principal modeling language for the proposed formalization, given its strengths and benefits, discussed thoroughly e.g. in Weilkiens [15] or Holt and Perry [25]. However, despite its robust modeling capabilities, SysML does not inherently offer the specific, quantifiable data required for simulation and analysis, as analyzed in [11]. Critical elements such as mass, power consumption of system components, and orbital parameters are essential for accurate simulations and system budgeting. To address this limitation, currently simulation tools must be fed with external mathematical databases that provide the detailed data necessary for these tasks.

caption_chunks.context: SysML elements, such as the above-mentioned Requirements and Blocks, are derived by applying stereotypes to existing UML elements, such as classes, making the SysML a specialization of the UML. An analogous approach has then been introduced for the proposed formalization, which therefore can be interpreted as a specialization of the SysML for CubeSats design activities. Through the introduction of several stereotypes, it becomes possible to specialize the SysML Block element into System, Component, Orbit, GroundStation or OperatingMode new elements, each one of them inheriting a standardized set of attributes for their characterization. An example of the Orbit element included with the proposed formalization is shown in Fig. 5. Fig. 5: Orbit UML stereotype example [9]. As shown in the Figure, it is created by applying a new stereotype to the UML Class «metaclass» - from which also the SysML Block element is originated - through an Extension $ ^{2} $ Relationship. By introducing such a stereotype, the designer can create any desired Orbit element by adding the appropriate values to the pre-defined set of attributes that the element will inherit (i.e., in this instance, the orbital parameters). More generally, once the stereotypes are incorporated into the model, they can be reused for various designs by simply adjusting the input data. Moreover, this approach does not limit the modeling capabilities of the SysML, since it is still possible to generate any desired element, diagram or connection in the model or to directly use the new elements in various diagrams like "classical" Blocks - without affecting the correctness of the model itself. 5 Discussion The application of UML stereotypes within the proposed formalization of the CubeSat SysML model provides several critical advantages that enhance the design process, data management, and overall efficiency of CubeSat development. These advantages are discussed throughout this section. One of the primary benefits of using this approach lies in the ability to create models that are both reusable and flexible. In the formalization proposed in [9], the stereotypes are designed to be generic yet sufficiently detailed to represent various CubeSat configurations. Once the stereotypes are integrated into the model, they can be reused across multiple designs without needing to recreate the structure or redefine attributes. Designers only need to update the specific data points, such as mass or power consumption, to reflect changes in the design or mission requirements. This flexibility is particularly valuable as iterative design processes are common, and multiple CubeSat missions may be developed simultaneously or sequentially. By maintaining a standardized framework using UML stereotypes, teams can reduce the time spent on manual model adjustments and focus on refining mission-specific details. Furthermore, the use of UML stereotypes facilitates identifying common structures in the model files, enabling the extraction of critical data for integration with any preferred set of simulation tools. This integration is achieved through the use of a dedicated parser, which leverages on the information conveyed by the stereotypes. Moreover, the parser - by knowing in advance the set of stereotypes and therefore the attributes introduced with them - automatically extracts the relevant data from the elements of the SysML model with a specific stereotype applied and converts them into a software-readable format. This reduces the risk of data fragmentation or inconsistencies across different tools and phases of the design process, ensuring that the CubeSat model remains the single source of truth throughout the PD phase without limiting the broader modeling capabilities of SysML, since it uses only the information relative to the stereotypes for data extraction, bypassing all other model's elements. The proposed set of stereotypes facilitates the automation of data extraction from the CubeSat model, streamlining the process of generating system budgets, performing trade-off studies, and conducting simulations. Once the relevant system parameters are defined using stereotypes, the model can be parsed to extract critical data such as: power consumptions, and mass estimates. This eliminates the need for manual data entry on each simulation tool, reducing the possibility of human error and significantly speeding up the design process. Moreover, the approach supports bidirectional data flow, meaning that updates from simulation results or parameter optimizations can be fed back into the SysML model automatically. For example, if a simulation tool determines an optimized power consumption profile, this data can be updated in the model without manual intervention. This automated update capability supports an agile and responsive design process, where the model is contin

With the same principles used for data extraction, the use of stereotypes in the formalization also supports the generation of dependency graphs as the one shown in Fig. 6, which visually depict the relationships between different system components and how changes in one parameter (e.g., mass or power consumption) affect other parts of the system. By knowing in advance the relationship between the data included within the stereotypes (e.g., system's power consumption and OMs overall power consumption), and by reading in the SysML the connections between the elements with specific stereotypes applied (e.g., composite associations between components and main systems), the data extraction process can automatically generate these graphs, which are particularly valuable for conducting trade-off studies during the PD phase. For example, the graph in Fig. 6 shows the connection between the masses of specific components and the Payload's overall mass, as well as the one between the system's power consumption and the consumptions of some OMs. Dependency graphs help designers understand the interdependencies within the CubeSat system and evaluate the impact of design changes. For example, increasing the power consumption of a system may require adjustments to the power budget, battery capacity, or solar array specifications. By visualizing these dependencies, designers can make more informed decisions and optimize system performance while managing trade-offs between competing design constraints. The integration of UML stereotypes into the CubeSat model also aligns with CE practices by supporting realtime collaboration among multidisciplinary teams. With the standardized data structure provided by stereotypes, different teams (e.g., power systems, communications, thermal management) can work concurrently on the same model, ensuring that their contributions are integrated seamlessly. The automated data extraction and update features also allow for continuous synchronization between the design model and simulation results, fostering a more dynamic and collaborative design process. While using stereotypes in the CubeSat SysML model formalization offers advantages, there are also some drawbacks and limitations. One of the primary drawbacks is the dependency on specific modeling tools, as discussed in Pons et al. [26]. The current framework was developed using Gaphor [27], an open-source modeling tool, and the parser designed for data extraction is tailored specifically to this tool. This creates limitations in terms of interoperability with other SysML tools, such as Papyrus [28] or Capella [29], which may store or structure their model files differently. As a result, the parser would require significant modification to be compatible with other tools, making the framework less flexible for users who prefer or are required to use different SysML platforms. This limitation reduces the broader applicability of the formalization, especially in environments where multiple tools are used or where teams need to switch between tools due to organizational requirements or project-specific needs. A temporary limitation is that the framework is focused solely on LEO CubeSat missions at the time being. Making it less suitable for complex missions involving non-nominal conditions, such as Early Orbit Phase (EOP) or off-nominal scenarios (e.g., detumbling or calibration). Customization for specialized missions can be time-consuming, especially when new stereotypes are required for novel subsystems, increasing the complexity of the model. The success of the approach heavily depends on the accuracy of the initial SysML model. Any inaccuracies or omissions can propagate through the system, leading to flawed simulations or incorrect system budgets. This necessitates thorough validation of the model, increasing the workload in the design phase. For larger teams, inconsistent application of stereotypes can cause data fragmentation, leading to synchronization issues across subsystems and complicating system-wide analyses. caption_chunks.context: 2.2 Model Based Systems Engineering Model-based systems engineering, or MBSE, is the formalized application of modeling to support tasks of a systems engineer including activities related to requirements, design, analysis, validation, and verification. This work begins in the conceptual design phase and continues on throughout development and later life cycle phases. [3] Figure 1 shows the phases of a typical design and the tasks which MBSE often aids in. Figure 1: MBSE across the System Life Cycle [3] MBSE is a term that describes an approach to Systems Engineering that emphasizes a system architecture model as the primary work artifact throughout the system development life cycle. A model is an approximation, representation, or idealization of selected aspects of the structure, behavior, or operation of a real world process, concept, or system. [4] A model usually offers different views in order to serve different purposes. A view is a representation of a system from the perspective of related concerns or issues. MBSE combines traditional systems engineering best practices with rigorous visual modeling techniques. Systems Engineers must interface with various other engineering specialties

caption_chunks.context: Figure 4: PolySat team member holds CP-6 mission [9] CubeSat missions can cost anywhere from fifty thousand dollars for a low-end satellite with limited functionality, up to multi-million dollars for a high-end satellite with multiple mission goals and associated instruments. The lower end of the spectrum is far below all other satellite design costs and has made the CubeSat a viable option for schools and universities across the world. Because of this, a large number of universities and some companies and government organizations around the world are developing CubeSats. A common design approach for CubeSat mission planning is to learn from previous design team knowledge and use intuition based trade studies for mission design. This can be dangerous if key personnel are unavailable, or operational parameters are neglected in the early stages of design. This often leads to cost and scheduling overruns, intolerable for a low budget CubeSat mission. However, these risks can be mitigated if standardized design practices, such as SysML, and standardized trade templates, such as HSF, are in place. Cal Poly's CubeSat design program is aptly named PolySat. Since their establishment, they have launch 7 missions, CP1 - CP6, and CP8. Cal Poly also designs the common deployment system called the Poly-PicoSatellite Orbital Deployer (P-POD). caption_chunks.context: The MagicDraw SysML plugin retains all capabilities of the MagicDraw architecture modeling environment with a System Engineer perspective. It includes SysML specific menus, toolbars, diagrams, specifications, user interface, dependency matrices, validation suites, etc. [17] The SysML plugin supports all SysML diagrams, including Requirements, Block Definition, Internal Blocks, Parametric and others. With this plugin, MagicDraw adds support for additional specification, analysis, design, and validation of a broad range of systems. 3.1.2 Model Quality Maintaining design consistency is a critical issue when concerning the complex nature of aerospace systems. Projects which lack consistency often end up suffering from cost and scheduling overruns. One solution to help mitigate these overruns is to use a standard for measuring the quality of a model. While there are multiple standards available, this work has been guided by and uses the "6 C's of MBSE." Figure 13 illustrates the 6C's and their relations to other possible elements which may be encountered while modeling. Figure 13: The 6C Model Quality Goals [18] The quality of models, whether being used for software development with UML or for satellite development with SysML, is often ascertained by following a set of six goals commonly referred to as the "6 C's of Model Based Systems Engineering." The elements of the 6 C's of MBSE are completeness, consistency, comprehensibility, confinement, and changeability. [18]

This was examined due to the fact that a user would have to acquire highly specialized knowledge of HSF and its extensive framework in order to execute a simulation. If the user could instead employ a more common modeling tool, SysML, as the input to HSF, then the ability to construct and run a simulation would be available to a larger user base. The user would then have the ability to use HSF to execute day in the life simulations and while also utilizing the benefits of MBSE from the SysML model.
